forces: Orchestra with piano, celesta and two harps
performers: Orchestre de la Suisse Romande; Ernest Ansermet
intro: In the second tableau of Petrushka, heard here in the 1911 original version, Petrushka is kicked into his room and left alone with his fury. Two clarinets play his cry, sounding C major and F♯ major together.

sections.label: A · Petrushka’s cry, clarinets and piano
sections.mNote: Two clarinets play clashing lines; the piano then takes over.

sections.label: B · Adagietto: piano, flutes and xylophone
sections.mNote: Adagietto for piano, flutes and xylophone.

sections.label: C · Petrushka dances for the Ballerina
sections.mNote: Allegro; he courts her with awkward leaps.

sections.label: D · Clarinet cadenza, piano arpeggios
sections.mNote: Clarinet cadenza over piano arpeggios after the Ballerina leaves

cues.title: C major and F♯ major clarinets
cues.text: A foot kicks Petrushka through the door. Two clarinets play arpeggios on C major and F♯ major together for his cry. The piano takes up the figure and runs it up and down the keyboard.
cues.evidence: Édition Russe full score, plate R.M.V. 127, pp. 63–65, rehearsals 48–51; stage direction and paired clarinet arpeggios. https://vmirror.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/1/18/IMSLP472771-PMLP179431-PMLUS00370-Stravinsky_-_Petrushka_OrchScore.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Scenery of the second tableau
cues.text: Petrushka’s room has black cardboard walls painted with stars and a crescent moon. A portrait of the magician hangs above the hole the puppet punches in the wall.
cues.evidence: The second tableau’s original scenery and action, transcribed in Helmut Kirchmeyer’s catalogue, K012, “Summary”. https://www.kcatalog.org/index.php/browse-chapters/kcatalog/179-k012-petrushka

cues.title: Adagietto, rehearsal 52
cues.text: The loud outburst stops. A piano run climbs into the Adagietto, where flutes repeat soft short figures and the xylophone plays with the piano’s high notes. Brass and strings rest.
cues.evidence: Édition Russe score, p. 67, rehearsal 52: piano quasi glissando, Adagietto, high woodwinds and xylophone; brass and strings rest. https://vmirror.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/1/18/IMSLP472771-PMLP179431-PMLUS00370-Stravinsky_-_Petrushka_OrchScore.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Origin of the second tableau
cues.text: Stravinsky wrote music for this unhappy puppet at the piano before the fairground scenes existed. By his own account, the piece he played to Diaghilev became the second tableau of Petrushka, and the rest of the ballet was built around it.
cues.evidence: Stravinsky’s account identifies the music played to Diaghilev as the future second tableau; reproduced by IRCAM. https://resources.ircam.fr/en/work/petrouchka

cues.title: Entrance of the Ballerina
cues.text: The Ballerina enters, and Petrushka tries to impress her. At Allegro, piano runs alternate with short wind phrases, and the metre changes from bar to bar. In the scenario his leaps alarm her, and she leaves.
cues.evidence: Édition Russe score, pp. 69–73, rehearsals 55–58: Ballerina’s entrance, Allegro and alternating metres. The scenario describes her alarm and departure. https://vmirror.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/1/18/IMSLP472771-PMLP179431-PMLUS00370-Stravinsky_-_Petrushka_OrchScore.pdf https://www.kcatalog.org/index.php/browse-chapters/kcatalog/179-k012-petrushka
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Clarinet cadenza, rehearsal 61
cues.text: The two clarinets bring back Petrushka’s cry in a slow cadenza. C major and F♯ major still sound together. The curtain closes on the same pair of chords that is associated with him at the beginning.
cues.evidence: Édition Russe score, p. 77, rehearsal 61: paired clarinet cadenza before the curtain passage. https://vmirror.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/1/18/IMSLP472771-PMLP179431-PMLUS00370-Stravinsky_-_Petrushka_OrchScore.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Piano run into the Adagietto
transitions.from: A · Petrushka’s cry, clarinets and piano
transitions.to: B · Adagietto: piano, flutes and xylophone
transitions.how: A held orchestral chord breaks off at a pause. At rehearsal 52 the piano plays a soft, rising run, close to a glissando, into the Adagietto. Flutes repeat a rocking figure above the piano’s low notes, and clarinets and xylophone add short taps. Brass and strings rest.

transitions.title: Flute and piano music to Allegro
transitions.from: B · Adagietto: piano, flutes and xylophone
transitions.to: C · Petrushka dances for the Ballerina
transitions.how: At rehearsals 55–56 (Édition Russe score, pp. 69–70) the music for flute and piano gives way to Allegro. Bassoons and oboes play repeated notes and the piano plays arpeggios. Bars of two crotchets alternate with bars of three. The strings move between pizzicato and arco while Petrushka dances.

transitions.title: Clarinet cadenza after the dance
transitions.from: C · Petrushka dances for the Ballerina
transitions.how: The dance stops. A solo clarinet extends its cadenza, marked molto ritardando and lamentoso assai, over held notes in the cellos. The piano then plays rushing arpeggios, and a call on the cor anglais follows.
transitions.evidence: Édition Russe score, pp. 73–74, after rehearsal 58. https://vmirror.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/1/18/IMSLP472771-PMLP179431-PMLUS00370-Stravinsky_-_Petrushka_OrchScore.pdf

source.title: Stravinsky, Petrushka, 1911 orchestration; Édition Russe plate R.M.V. 127, Dover reprint
source.locator: Printed pp. 63–77, rehearsals 48–61. Public-domain score in the US, not the EU. Passage timings are provisional, guided by cache/analysis/stravinsky-petrushka-room.txt. Xylophone is grouped under percussion; active groups describe a passage, not every simultaneous note.

timeline.note: After the opening ejection, Petrushka’s paired clarinets and piano enter.
timeline.evidence: Score pp. 63–64; opening active sound, with reduced level through 0:10–0:40.

timeline.note: Exposed clarinet figures and piano arpeggios carry the puppet’s complaint.
timeline.evidence: Score p. 64, rehearsal 49; boundary at 0:30, before the growth in activity at 0:45.

timeline.note: The Furioso gives the complaint to a larger body of wind, brass and strings.
timeline.evidence: Score pp. 65–67, rehearsal 51; crest at 1:00–1:05 and boundary at 1:12.

timeline.note: Adagietto reduces the sound to piano, high winds and xylophone.
timeline.evidence: Score p. 67, rehearsal 52; 1:12 boundary and low relative level at 1:15–1:30.

timeline.note: Andantino and the following visit preparation place a quieter line over the piano.
timeline.evidence: Score pp. 68–69, rehearsals 53–55; 1:56 boundary, before the changed balance at 2:18. Groups vary within the passage.

timeline.note: The visit’s Allegro spreads animated gestures across piano, winds, brass and strings.
timeline.evidence: Score pp. 70–73, rehearsals 56–58; 2:46 change, attack density 4.4/s at 2:45, and increasing level towards 3:00. Combinations change within the passage.

timeline.note: After the visit, piano and short wind gestures begin the final complaint.
timeline.evidence: Score pp. 73–74, rehearsals 58–59; quiet interval at 3:10–3:15 after the 3:08 boundary.

timeline.note: The last withdrawal includes the clarinets’ slow cadenza before the curtain passage.
timeline.evidence: Score p. 77, rehearsal 61; relative-level retreat after 3:55 and boundary at 4:04. The list covers the changing closing combinations, not a continuous tutti.

fields.value: Underlying 1911 composition and original 1912 score are public domain in the United States; the ordinary EU life-plus-70 composition term has not expired.
fields.note: Stravinsky died in 1971, giving an ordinary EU term through 31 December 2041. This is a territorial term calculation, not worldwide clearance, and it does not grant rights in modern editions, stage designs or choreography. The viewable score is hosted in the US; recording-term eligibility below does not clear the underlying composition.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Rule 3 — first lawful publication anywhere before 1963: London CS 6009, commercially published by 1958. Territorial EU sound-recording basis only; US sound-recording status is not established.
fields.note: A contemporary London/Pecar Electronics advertisement in the Grosse Pointe News, 6 November 1958, p. 7, pictures this Petrushka/Ansermet cover with catalogue CS 6009 under recordings NOW AVAILABLE. This directly establishes commercial availability in 1958; Archive’s 1958 carrier date and Decca’s ℗ 1958 attribution corroborate it. The rule concerns first lawful publication anywhere, not first EU publication; the US advertisement is therefore pertinent. A 1958 lawful publication exhausted the former 50-year EU performance/phonogram term by the end of 2008, before the 1 November 2013 protection threshold for the 70-year extension. The exact earliest market/day and any earlier issue are not established or required for this pre-1963 finding. No CC licence, worldwide public-domain claim, or US recording clearance is asserted.

composer.born: 17 June 1882, Oranienbaum, near St Petersburg, Russia
composer.epithet: Composer of dance music in which a single displaced accent could unsettle the dancers, and of a psalm setting that scarcely moves.
facts: Diaghilev’s Ballets Russes · Ramuz’s travelling theatre · Balanchine · Auden and Kallman
Ballets, operas, symphonies and sacred music; composing and recording into his eighties
composer.background:
Stravinsky was born in 1882 at Oranienbaum. His father, Fyodor, sang bass at the Mariinsky Theatre in St Petersburg; Igor heard him on stage and began piano lessons at nine. He entered St Petersburg University to study law. There he befriended Vladimir Rimsky-Korsakov, whose father heard his first pieces in 1902. Rimsky-Korsakov took him on privately, giving regular lessons from 1905 until his death in 1908. The pupil orchestrated pages of Pan Voyevoda, then had to explain why his teacher had scored them differently.

He married his cousin Catherine Nossenko in 1906; by 1914 they had four children. His E♭ Symphony owed much to Glazunov and Tchaikovsky; Scherzo fantastique and Fireworks are short orchestral works. Sergei Diaghilev heard his music in 1909 and gave him some Chopin to orchestrate for Les Sylphides. A full ballet, The Firebird, followed. Stravinsky handed over the score in sections while Michel Fokine worked out the dances. In his 1936 autobiography he recalled that the rehearsals ended with dinner beside Diaghilev and Nijinsky, and good claret.
